name: Wardaman
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_quote: a major stress, characterizable in terms of greater loudness and generally higher pitch, falls on the penultimate syllable of the inflected word

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (outside the strict set, out-code lexical; in the dominant set; penultimate stress kept as the dominant pattern)
audit.reasoning: Source side is as good as it gets: the deciding work is the 617-pp Mouton reference grammar (1994), the whole stress section (pp. 53-56) is held as page scan, and the deciding quotation is verbatim on p. 53. The risk is not the source but the register. The catalog carries Wardaman as fixed-strict (in the strict set True, 'verified-clean' from this search of works with stress in the title, never owner-reviewed), and the strict set is defined as 'one exceptionless weight-blind pattern per word length; a stated exception removes it'. The same held pages state exceptions in Merlan's own words: p. 53 'it is clear that there are different stress patterns within particular word classes, which must be recognized as part of the phonological structure of roots.. For nouns, we must distinguish at least two different stress patterns.. Among three-syllable and some longer words there is also a second pattern of ante-penultimate stress'
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again.— confirmed independently. I re-read the page scan (not just the scanned), and the scanned of PA54. p.53 carries both record sentences verbatim ('The most general word-level pattern in Wardaman is that a major stress, characterizable in terms of greater loudness and generally higher pitch, falls on the penultimate syllable of the inflected word.
